genZNote: No cell wall means beta-lactams do absolutely nothing to it — and the urea-splitting is right there in the name.

morphology.shape: Highly pleomorphic — lacks a cell wall entirely
morphology.size: ~0.1-0.3 µm — among the smallest known free-living bacteria
morphology.notes: Lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall entirely (like Mycoplasma) — does not Gram stain and is intrinsically resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics

habitat.hostAssociation: Can be a normal genital tract commensal or an opportunistic pathogen, particularly in the neonatal and reproductive context
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Primarily host-associated; sexually transmitted between adults

microscopy.stain: Does not Gram stain (no cell wall); not typically visualized directly

culture.media: Specialized broth/agar (e.g., 10B broth, A8 agar) containing urea and serum
culture.growthCharacteristics: Fastidious; requires special media and CO2-enriched atmosphere; distinguished from Mycoplasma by urease production
culture.colonyMorphology: Very small colonies, sometimes described as tiny 'fried egg'-like colonies under magnification, though generally smaller/less distinct than Mycoplasma colonies

identificationClues: Lacks a cell wall entirely — does not Gram stain and is intrinsically resistant to penicillins/cephalosporins
Urease positive — the defining biochemical feature that distinguishes the genus from Mycoplasma
Recovered from genital tract specimens using specialized culture media (10B broth/A8 agar) or PCR
Associated with adverse neonatal outcomes when transmitted vertically to preterm infants

diseases: Associated with chorioamnionitis and preterm birth
Neonatal complications in preterm infants, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia and, rarely, meningitis
virulenceFactors: Urease production, generating ammonia that may contribute to tissue irritation and possibly urinary stone formation
Lack of a cell wall, allowing intracellular-adjacent persistence and intrinsic antibiotic resistance to cell-wall-targeting drugs
clinicalImportance.transmission: Sexual contact in adults; vertical transmission from mother to fetus/neonate (in utero or during vaginal delivery)
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: A frequent genital tract commensal in sexually active adults, making causal attribution to disease sometimes difficult; of particular concern in preterm neonates due to associations with chorioamnionitis and neonatal lung disease
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Because Ureaplasma lacks a cell wall, beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins) are completely ineffective — macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones are used instead

examFacts.importantDisease: Nongonococcal urethritis; neonatal complications in preterm infants
examFacts.importantTest: Culture on specialized urea-containing media (10B/A8) or PCR
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A cell-wall-less genital mycoplasma distinguished from Mycoplasma by urease production — intrinsically resistant to all beta-lactam antibiotics
